paragraphs: Stochastic gradient methods can support approximate sampling and uncertainty estimates, but choosing their settings is difficult. Existing guidance can become quantitatively inaccurate with large batches or when the statistical model does not correctly describe the data. This paper develops approximations intended to make tuning reliable in these challenging settings.

The approach analyzes updates in discrete time, retaining the step-by-step structure of the algorithms. It covers stochastic gradient descent and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, both with and without momentum. The resulting predictions describe the spread of individual iterates, the uncertainty of averaged iterates, and how strongly successive iterates remain correlated.

The authors also prove quantitative error bounds that do not depend solely on an infinite-sample limit, supporting the approximations’ usefulness for practical uncertainty quantification. Numerical experiments show improved tuning guidance across models and data-generating distributions where existing approaches fail. These include robust inference using beta-divergence instead of log-loss, extending the reported usefulness beyond conventional likelihood-based analysis.
icml-2026-accurate-large-sample-uncertai.tldr: Discrete-time analysis improves tuning and uncertainty estimates for stochastic gradient sampling, including large-batch and misspecified-model settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies how connections among neurons within a network can help visual representations adapt to input quality. The authors train stabilized supralinear networks on natural images using local plasticity rules. Their focus is strong lateral connections that combine excitatory influences, which encourage activity, with inhibitory influences, which suppress it.

These connections allow the network to move between different dynamical regimes. With noisy or low-contrast inputs, it recruits more neurons to extract features through population coding. At high contrast, it uses a much smaller active population, producing sparse coding. Previous experiments and models have associated this reduction in activity with lower metabolic demand; the abstract does not report a direct energy measurement here.

The model shows greater robustness and adaptability under degraded inputs than sparse coding, independent component analysis, and other unsupervised models. That advantage disappears when the lateral connections are removed. This comparison supports the proposed role of excitatory–inhibitory recurrence in changing coding strategies with input conditions, offering a concrete visual example of adaptive representation learning.
icml-2026-adaptive-coding-emerges-in-sta.tldr: Excitatory and inhibitory lateral connections let a visual network switch coding strategies with input quality and improve robustness to degraded images.

paragraphs: AgentNoiseBench examines whether tool-using language-model agents remain effective when their surroundings are imperfect. Conventional benchmarks often assume cleaner interactions than deployment provides. The paper argues that overlooking uncertainty and environmental noise leaves an important gap between benchmark evaluation and the conditions agents encounter outside those evaluations.

The authors organize environmental noise into two broad categories: noise associated with users and noise associated with tools. They then build an automated pipeline that adds controllable noise to existing agent benchmarks while keeping the tasks solvable. Preserving solvability matters because the evaluation can probe an agent’s response to disruption without simply making successful completion impossible.

Using this pipeline, the authors evaluate models spanning different architectures and parameter scales. They find consistent performance variations across noise conditions, showing that current agents are sensitive to realistic perturbations. The contribution is a systematic way to measure that sensitivity and compare behavior under controlled environmental changes. The stated findings concern robustness evaluation rather than a proposed training method that eliminates the observed weaknesses.
icml-2026-agentnoisebench-benchmarking-r.tldr: AgentNoiseBench adds controlled user and tool noise to solvable benchmarks to measure how robustly language-model agents handle imperfect environments.

paragraphs: Multimodal sentiment analysis combines different signals to infer emotion, but some signals may be missing because of sensor failures, corrupted data, or privacy concerns. Existing recovery methods can require expensive generators and introduce semantic drift. Methods that avoid recovery can instead rely on static mappings that miss the emotional details of individual samples.

Adaptive Prototype Imputation addresses both problems with reference representations that can be adjusted for each instance. Its SCOPE component constructs non-trainable class-temporal prototypes to provide stable semantic anchors. These anchors supply class-level structure, helping the missing-modality representation remain connected to the sentiment information the model needs.

The DIAM component then adapts those anchors using direction-specific affine transformations. This allows the representation to reflect the particular sample without introducing a heavy generative recovery process. Experiments on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI report better performance than state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support combining stable prototypes with instance-dependent adjustments as a lightweight approach to sentiment analysis when some modalities are unavailable.
icml-2026-api-adaptive-prototype-imputat.tldr: API adapts stable sentiment prototypes to individual samples, handling missing modalities without heavy generative reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to reuse the computation already invested in pretrained language models when building larger ones. Its starting point is a converged mixture-of-experts model. Rather than leaving the checkpoint at its original size, the proposed strategy expands its architecture and then continues training, carrying previous learning into a larger model.

The expansion proceeds along two dimensions. Interpositional layer copying increases depth, while duplicating experts with added noise increases width. The authors call this orthogonal growth. Together, these operations provide a way to enlarge an existing mixture-of-experts checkpoint instead of requiring the larger architecture to learn everything from an untrained starting point.

Scaling-law analysis finds a strong positive correlation between prior training investment and final accuracy. Experiments involving models up to 70 billion parameters and one trillion tokens report a 10.6% accuracy improvement over training from scratch with the same additional compute budget. That comparison concerns new computation after checkpoint reuse; it does not equate the total historical computation invested in the two approaches.
icml-2026-beyond-sunk-costs-boosting-llm.tldr: Expanding pretrained mixture-of-experts models in depth and width improves reported accuracy over training from scratch under equal additional compute budgets.

paragraphs: An image can contain several objects with different sizes and contexts, making recognition difficult when the model summarizes everything in one global representation. This paper identifies that summary, the CLS token, as a bottleneck for multi-label recognition in vision-language models such as CLIP. Relevant evidence for separate labels can become mixed together.

PIAA instead makes predictions at the image-patch level and then combines them adaptively. It improves patch predictions in two ways: reducing semantic entanglement in visual representations and constructing an unsupervised visual classifier to narrow the gap between visual and language features. The aggregation module consolidates these local scores into a prediction containing multiple labels.

The entire pipeline operates without gradient updates or parameter fine-tuning, despite including an unsupervised classifier construction step. Experiments report strong gains with little additional computation, including more than a 6% mAP gain over representative baselines on NUS-WIDE. The result supports preserving and combining local evidence when a single image contains several distinct recognition targets.
icml-2026-cls-is-not-enough-multi-label-.tldr: PIAA improves training-free multi-label recognition by predicting from image patches and adaptively combining their evidence.

paragraphs: CombinationTS asks which parts of a forecasting model actually account for its performance. The paper argues that increasingly complex architectures can receive credit for gains that are statistically fragile or caused by other components. Its proposed evaluation framework therefore shifts attention from ranking complete models to attributing effects to individual modules.

The framework separates a model into input transformation, embedding, encoder, decoder, and output transformation. It compares these modules within a shared space of evaluation conditions. Each component is described through marginalized performance and stability, so assessment reflects behavior across conditions rather than resting on a single favorable result. Large-scale paired evaluations support the comparisons.

The central finding is what the authors call the Identity Paradox: with a well-designed embedding, a parameter-free identity encoder often matches or exceeds complex backbones. This is a conditional empirical finding, not a claim that encoders never help. It suggests that the way data is presented to a model can explain gains otherwise attributed to its central processing architecture.
icml-2026-combinationts-a-modular-framew.tldr: CombinationTS attributes forecasting performance to individual modules and finds that good embeddings often let an identity encoder match complex backbones.

paragraphs: Coordinating with an unfamiliar partner requires adapting to how that partner behaves. Training against diverse populations can improve robustness, but may leave agents poorly equipped for behavior outside their training distribution. Fine-tuning also requires interactions before it produces meaningful improvement. CooT addresses this problem through adaptation within the model’s context.

Coordination Transformers are trained on trajectories from agents with behavioral preferences. From these examples, they learn to align their actions with a partner’s intentions through observation. The target of generalization is partner behavior: the model adjusts how it collaborates without updating its parameters as it encounters a new partner.

Evaluations on Overcooked and Google Research Football report consistent advantages over population-based methods, gradient-based fine-tuning, and Meta-RL baselines. Human evaluations also favor CooT as a collaborator. Ablations show rapid adaptation to new partners and stability when partners change suddenly. These results support the usefulness of in-context partner adaptation for the evaluated coordination tasks and motivate its application to human–AI collaboration.
icml-2026-coot-learning-to-coordinate-in.tldr: CooT learns to adapt to unfamiliar partners through observation and context, achieving rapid coordination without parameter updates.

paragraphs: Scientific datasets often mix scarce, accurate measurements with larger collections of less accurate labels. Learning from both is difficult when their biases are complex and the datasets cover different inputs. Many multi-fidelity methods rely on the same samples having labels at multiple fidelity levels, a pairing that can be unavailable in practice.

This paper proposes an end-to-end framework that does not require paired samples. It separates label supervision into three complementary sources of trusted information: absolute values from high-fidelity labels, reliable high- and medium-fidelity intervals governed by adaptive constraints, and numerical ordering relationships within a fidelity level. Each source captures a different kind of usable label information.

The unified model combines these subsets to make use of medium- and low-fidelity data without treating every label as equally accurate. Experiments on molecular and material property benchmarks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-fidelity and single-fidelity baselines. The reported robustness under unpaired conditions supports extracting trustworthy relationships from heterogeneous labels when direct cross-fidelity matching is impractical.
icml-2026-credible-information-subset-de.tldr: The framework learns from unpaired scientific data of varying accuracy by combining trustworthy label values, intervals, and ordering relationships.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised continual learning asks a model to learn expanding sets of classes from a stream containing both labeled and unlabeled data. Predictions on unlabeled examples can provide supervision, but incorrect pseudo-labels can also reinforce mistakes. The paper focuses on how this process can increase interference between previously learned classes and newly arriving ones.

DiL organizes updates around reliable discrete anchors that remain stable under noisy pseudo-labels. Its Discrete Contrastive Distillation component makes knowledge transfer selective and references those anchors, rather than indiscriminately distilling information from unlabeled examples. This is intended to curb the repeated reinforcement of unreliable predictions while preserving useful guidance for continual updates.

A second component, Class-Aware Channel-Chunked Encoding, divides representations into channel chunks. It uses the confusion matrix produced by the discrete anchors to help distinguish new classes from older classes they resemble. Across multiple datasets and semi-supervised continual-learning protocols, the authors report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support jointly controlling unreliable supervision and separating confusing classes as the class set grows.
icml-2026-dil-discrete-anchored-represen.tldr: DiL uses stable discrete anchors and class-aware representations to reduce error reinforcement and interference during semi-supervised continual learning.

paragraphs: Improving a generator’s average reward does not directly control its unusually poor or unusually good outputs. These extremes serve different purposes: reducing low-reward outcomes supports reliability, while emphasizing rare high-reward outcomes supports discovery. Tail-aware Flow Fine-Tuning gives these two objectives an explicit role in adapting pretrained flow models.

The method uses Conditional Value-at-Risk, or CVaR, to target a selected reward tail. Right-CVaR emphasizes high-reward samples, while left-CVaR addresses low-reward samples. A variational dual formulation splits the optimization into two decoupled stages: a lightweight search for a one-dimensional threshold and one entropy-regularized fine-tuning process driven by a specially constructed pseudo-reward.

This decomposition makes tail-directed fine-tuning computationally comparable to standard methods focused on expected reward. The authors demonstrate effectiveness in illustrative experiments, high-dimensional text-to-image generation, and molecular design. The contribution is a practical mechanism for choosing which part of the outcome distribution to improve, rather than expecting an increase in average reward to shape the extremes appropriately.
icml-2026-efficient-tail-aware-generativ.tldr: TFFT efficiently fine-tunes flow models to favor exceptional outputs or reduce poor ones by explicitly optimizing reward-distribution tails.

paragraphs: Fern approaches long-horizon forecasting through the geometry of how a model transforms its inputs. The authors argue that matching conditional means is insufficient and that local Jacobians need explicit spectral structure. These Jacobians describe local changes in the forecasting map, making their structure relevant to how predictions stretch and evolve.

Using Brenier’s theorem, Fern directly parameterizes the Jacobian through a symmetric positive semidefinite factorization. It treats forecasting as optimal transport from a fixed Gaussian source to data-dependent ellipsoids. Efficient Householder-based orthogonal factors avoid a separate eigendecomposition of dense Jacobians, while exposing interpretable measurements of local stretching, spectral radius, and volume change.

The authors also introduce synthetic stress tests with nonstationary shocks, Wasserstein-based shape metrics, and Effective Prediction Time. In these settings, Fern shows exceptional stability and reported advantages of over two orders of magnitude, reaching up to 790 times, against baselines including DLinear and Koopa. The stated gains concern the nonstationary evaluations designed to reveal brittleness that standard benchmarks may miss.
icml-2026-ellipsoidal-time-series-foreca.tldr: Fern structures forecasting transformations through ellipsoidal geometry and reports large stability gains in synthetic tests with nonstationary shocks.

paragraphs: Camera-controlled video generation often uses an anchor video to show the desired camera motion. Rendering these anchors from estimated point clouds and camera trajectories can introduce misalignment, forcing the generator to compensate during training. EPiC changes how training anchors are constructed so that guidance aligns closely with the source video.

The framework masks source videos according to what is visible in their first frame. This produces training anchors without estimating camera poses or point clouds. A lightweight Anchor-ControlNet then feeds guidance from visible regions into a pretrained video diffusion model, adding less than 1% to its parameter count. The design reduces the burden of learning from inaccurate rendered guidance.

The authors report efficient training with fewer parameters, steps, and data, plus state-of-the-art image-to-video camera control on RealEstate10K and MiraData. At test time, the model generalizes to anchors rendered from point clouds, enabling 3D-informed control despite the different training construction. It also shows strong zero-shot generalization to video-to-video scenarios, extending the reported usefulness beyond its image-to-video evaluation.
icml-2026-epic-efficient-video-camera-co.tldr: EPiC learns efficient camera control from precisely aligned masked-video anchors and transfers to point-cloud guidance at test time.

paragraphs: Combining modalities requires keeping complementary information while suppressing noise specific to each source. Information Bottleneck methods address this by encouraging task-relevant representations. The paper identifies two shortcomings in existing multimodal versions: they mainly constrain the fused representation, and they can depend on restrictive assumptions about the distribution of latent features.

IBMA applies the Information Bottleneck principle both to the fused representation and to each modality’s own representation. Its alignment mechanism guides each encoder toward information that is useful for the task and consistent with the complementary modality. This brings cross-modal semantic agreement into the individual representations, rather than addressing it only after fusion.

The authors also derive an efficient, distribution-free variational upper bound for the bottleneck loss. This avoids the specified latent-distribution assumptions and can be optimized with standard stochastic gradient descent. Extensive experiments report better performance than existing multimodal learning methods. Together, the results support aligning modality-specific representations while controlling irrelevant information at both the individual and fused levels.
icml-2026-ibma-information-bottleneck-ba.tldr: IBMA aligns individual and fused multimodal representations using an Information Bottleneck objective without restrictive latent-distribution assumptions.

paragraphs: Streaming-data methods need uncertainty estimates as well as fast parameter updates. Although first-order updates can be inexpensive, their covariance calculations still require quadratic time and memory in the parameter dimension. Newton methods offer a second-order alternative, but solving their systems directly introduces a cubic computational bottleneck.

The paper studies an online Newton method with Hessian averaging and an approximate solver based on accelerated sketch-and-project steps. Nesterov’s acceleration helps bring the computation to the quadratic scale associated with first-order inference. The analysis explicitly accounts for uncertainty from both incoming random data and the randomized computation used to approximate each Newton direction.

Under standard smoothness and moment conditions, the authors prove global almost-sure convergence and asymptotic normality of the last iterate. They characterize its limiting covariance through a Lyapunov equation and provide a fully online covariance estimator with non-asymptotic guarantees. Regression experiments report superior online inference, supporting the combination of approximate second-order updates with uncertainty estimates that include solver randomness.
icml-2026-inference-of-online-newton-met.tldr: Accelerated sketching makes online Newton inference computationally practical while quantifying uncertainty from both streaming data and randomized computation.

paragraphs: This work connects evaluation of generated videos with evaluation of how models interpret those videos. Its AIGVE-60K benchmark covers 3,050 prompts across 20 fine-grained task dimensions. It contains 58,500 videos from 30 text-to-video models, with 120,000 human mean-opinion scores and 60,000 annotated question-answer pairs supporting these complementary assessments.

Built on that dataset, LOVE is a large-multimodal-model-based evaluation metric. It assesses perceptual preference, correspondence between text and video, and accuracy on the particular task. These dimensions separate whether a video is visually appealing from whether it follows the requested content and fulfills the task, allowing evaluation to capture more than one aspect of quality.

The authors then use LOVE as the basis for LOVE-Reward, which optimizes text-to-video models through reinforcement learning. Experiments report state-of-the-art evaluation performance and effective generalization across generated-video benchmarks. LOVE-Reward also improves generated-video quality and text correspondence. The overall contribution links human-annotated benchmarking, automated evaluation, and a reward signal for improving generation.
icml-2026-love-benchmarking-and-evaluati.tldr: LOVE combines a human-annotated video benchmark, a multidimensional evaluation metric, and a reinforcement-learning reward that improves video generation.

paragraphs: A prediction set expresses uncertainty by covering an unknown outcome with a guaranteed probability. That guarantee alone does not determine which action a decision-maker should take. This paper develops a framework that evaluates decisions against the worst-case outcome distribution compatible with the set’s coverage guarantee, explicitly accounting for the consequences of mistakes.

For a fixed prediction set, the authors characterize the minimax-optimal policy. It balances the worst possible loss within the set against a penalty for losses when the outcome falls outside it. They then use this decision rule to derive how prediction sets themselves should be constructed to minimize robust risk while satisfying a coverage constraint.

Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction turns this objective into a practical algorithm while maintaining finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage. Evaluations on medical diagnosis and a toy static hazard-decision benchmark report fewer critical mistakes than baselines, especially when out-of-set errors are expensive. The findings show why a set’s usefulness can depend on downstream loss, beyond whether it meets the required coverage level.
icml-2026-optimal-decision-making-based-.tldr: ROCP constructs coverage-guaranteed prediction sets around downstream decision costs, reducing critical errors in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Video anomaly detectors need information about unusual events, but their internal representations can also retain sensitive details about people. This paper introduces an Orthogonal Projection Layer that removes task-irrelevant variation and concentrates representations on anomaly-related cues. Its goal is to make privacy considerations part of the representation design.

For scenes involving people, Guided OPL specifically suppresses facial attributes while preserving non-identifying features such as pose and motion. It uses weak supervision indicating whether a face is present, rather than identity labels. A cosine alignment objective encourages consistent identification and removal of facial information without requiring adversarial training.

The authors also propose an evaluation framework that measures detection performance alongside privacy preservation and examines how sensitive information is filtered. Experiments show reductions in sensitive information while detection accuracy is maintained or improved. These results support projection-based representations as a practical privacy-aware design for anomaly detection. The stated outcome is reduced sensitive information, rather than a guarantee that all identifying information has been eliminated.
icml-2026-privacy-aware-video-anomaly-de.tldr: Guided orthogonal projection suppresses facial information in video representations while maintaining or improving anomaly-detection accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Probabilistic bisection extends binary search to situations where responses can be wrong, making it useful for problems such as locating a root with noisy feedback. Although the algorithm has worked well empirically, its convergence speed lacked a clear theoretical account. This paper establishes a geometric convergence rate.

Geometric convergence means that error contracts at an exponential rate as the procedure progresses. The authors characterize this rate as optimal because it matches the rate achieved by classical binary search with noiseless responses. This comparison concerns convergence speed; it does not imply that noise disappears or that the procedures have identical behavior at every step.

The proof directly studies the dynamics of the algorithm’s queries. Those queries move back and forth around the true answer while steadily getting closer, yielding an estimator that rapidly concentrates near the truth. By analyzing this movement, the paper supplies a theoretical explanation for the algorithm’s observed efficiency. The authors also suggest that these analytical techniques may be useful independently for studying probabilistic bisection dynamics.
icml-2026-probabilistic-bisection-algori.tldr: The paper proves geometric convergence for probabilistic bisection by showing how its noisy queries oscillate toward the true answer.

paragraphs: RA-Det detects generated images by examining their response to controlled changes. The paper identifies robustness asymmetry: under small, structured perturbations, natural images maintain more stable semantic representations, while generated images exhibit larger feature drift. This provides a behavioral signal as visible signs of generation become harder to distinguish.

The authors develop a theoretical lower bound connecting this asymmetry to memorization tendencies in generative models, offering an explanation for its occurrence across architectures. RA-Det turns the difference in representation stability into a detection signal. It requires no generator fingerprints and is described as data- and model-agnostic, with transfer to generators unseen during evaluation setup.

Across 14 generative models and comparisons with more than 10 strong detectors, RA-Det reports superior results and a 12.92% improvement in average performance. These findings support robustness asymmetry as a broadly useful detection cue across the tested generators. The central contribution is making controlled probing useful for detection, rather than depending only on what an unmodified image looks like.
icml-2026-ra-det-towards-universal-detec.tldr: RA-Det detects generated images through their greater semantic feature drift under controlled perturbations, with reported transfer to unseen generators.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can lose some of the risk recognition their language components exhibit when processing text alone. The paper attributes this partly to visual inputs weakening risk-related signals. Risk Awareness Injection aims to restore those signals without safety fine-tuning or broad token changes that can be costly or reduce task usefulness.

The method builds an Unsafe Prototype Subspace from language embeddings, providing a representation of unsafe content. It then selectively modulates visual tokens identified as high risk to activate safety-relevant signals in the shared visual-language feature space. The intervention is designed to preserve the tokens’ original semantic content so that cross-modal reasoning remains useful.

RAI is lightweight and requires no training. Across multiple jailbreak and utility benchmarks, experiments show substantial reductions in attack success without compromising task performance. The findings support targeted feature modulation as a way to improve safety calibration while retaining capability in the evaluated tasks. Its mechanism centers on amplifying existing risk recognition rather than learning an entirely new safety response through additional training.
icml-2026-risk-awareness-injection-calib.tldr: RAI amplifies risk signals in selected visual tokens without training, reducing jailbreak success while preserving benchmark task performance.

paragraphs: Local explanations approximate a black-box model near a particular example using a simpler model. LIME uses a sparse linear approximation, but feature effects can change even within a small neighborhood. A single linear effect can then misrepresent the model, while a separate feature-selection objective can add instability when local samples change.

PL-LIME replaces each feature’s single linear effect with an instance-anchored piecewise linear function. This permits changes in local behavior while retaining a limited explanation budget. Its two stages use consistent objectives, addressing the mismatch between selecting features and fitting their effects that the authors identify in LIME.

Sparsity comes from nonnegative shrinkage that directly scales estimated local effects, keeping the explanation compact while aiming to preserve interpretability and stability. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report higher local fidelity and greater stability than LIME. The resulting explanations capture finer variations in nearby feature effects, supporting a modest increase in surrogate flexibility when a straight-line approximation is too restrictive.
icml-2026-sparse-and-faithful-local-expl.tldr: PL-LIME uses sparse piecewise linear feature effects to produce more faithful and stable local explanations than LIME in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Natural language contains a few frequent skills and many rare ones. It may therefore seem helpful to flatten the training distribution so that rare skills appear more often. This paper reports the opposite result across a range of compositional reasoning tasks: power-law sampling consistently outperforms uniform sampling, including in state tracking and multi-step arithmetic.

To investigate why, the authors introduce a minimal skill-composition task and prove that learning under a power-law distribution requires substantially less training data in that setting. Their analysis attributes the advantage to an asymmetry in sampling that improves a problematic loss landscape, making the learning process more favorable.

Frequent skill combinations become easier to acquire first, and those learned combinations provide a stepping stone toward rare skills. This mechanism offers an explanation for why unequal frequencies can help compositional learning rather than simply disadvantage the long tail. The empirical results and simplified theoretical task challenge the intuition that uniformity is always preferable, without establishing that every training problem benefits from a power-law distribution.
icml-2026-the-power-of-power-law-asymmet.tldr: Power-law training distributions improve compositional reasoning in the studied tasks by letting frequent skill combinations support learning of rarer ones.

paragraphs: Uniform discrete diffusion models offer a way to generate discrete outputs, but directly applying Group Relative Policy Optimization produces unstable training and only modest gains. UDM-GRPO adapts reinforcement learning to this model family by reconsidering which output is treated as the action and how training trajectories are reconstructed.

The framework treats the final clean sample as the action, providing a more accurate and stable optimization signal. It reconstructs trajectories through the forward diffusion process so that probability paths align better with the pretraining distribution. Two additional strategies, Reduced-Step and CFG-Free, further improve training efficiency.

Across multiple text-to-image tasks, the authors report substantial improvements over the base model. GenEval accuracy rises from 69% to 96%, while PickScore increases from 20.46 to 23.81, with reported state-of-the-art performance across continuous and discrete settings. OCR benchmark accuracy also increases from 8% to 57%. These results support adapting the reinforcement-learning formulation to the diffusion model’s structure instead of applying GRPO unchanged.
icml-2026-udm-grpo-stable-and-efficient-.tldr: UDM-GRPO stabilizes reinforcement learning for uniform discrete diffusion models and delivers large reported gains on text-to-image and OCR benchmarks.

paragraphs: An image’s overall aesthetic score reflects several attributes whose importance varies with content and use. When a model learns only from overall scores, these influences become blended. The paper argues that samples dominated by different attributes can then produce conflicting gradients, partially canceling learning signals and leaving systematic prediction biases.

AGREE addresses this by learning attribute-specific representation subspaces and routing gradients according to each sample’s sensitivity to different attributes. It estimates that sensitivity through perturbation analysis. Semantic anchors further reduce coupling between attributes, while error-aware reweighting improves robustness. Together, these components aim to make training updates respect the different sources of aesthetic judgment.

Experiments on AVA, LAPIS, AADB, TAD66K, and PARA show consistent improvements across diverse aesthetic-assessment baselines. AGREE can be added to existing end-to-end methods without changing their original architectures. The findings support treating disagreement among attribute-driven training signals as a concrete optimization problem, helping explain why learning from a single overall score can require more structured handling of its underlying influences.
icml-2026-when-attributes-disagree-gradi.tldr: AGREE improves image aesthetic assessment by routing gradients according to sample-specific attribute sensitivity and reducing conflicts among training signals.
